description: AstroPumas es un equipo apasionado por la tecnología, la ingeniería y la exploración de nuevas ideas. Creado por estudiantes de Ingeniería en Computación de la ENES Mérida, UNAM, nos encanta investigar, desarrollar software y aplicar el código para construir soluciones creativas de alto impacto. Nuestro objetivo es trabajar juntos, aprender en el proceso y desarrollar un proyecto innovador y funcional.
summary: Space Junk Explorers is an educational and interactive web platform that introduces children to the challenge of objects and equipment left on the Moon and Mars after space missions. It transforms NASA scientific information and historical mission records into an exploration experience designed from a child's perspective [1, 4–6]. The project began by listening to Josue, a 7-year-old child who imagined how he wanted to discover these worlds: piloting a spacecraft, finding machines, and becoming an astronaut. His ideas inspired an adventure featuring interactive maps, missions, clues, mini-games, and collectible badges. Our goal is to spark scientific curiosity, encourage learning through play, and raise awareness of the legacy of space exploration. Our philosophy is simple: children are not just the audience for the science of the future; they can also help design it.
details:
For decades, space missions have left objects, instruments, components, and equipment on the surfaces of the Moon and Mars. Published estimates for the Moon place the amount of human-made material at approximately 180,000–181,000 kg [2, 3]. However, there is no consolidated official total: NASA’s catalog records artifacts and locations but does not provide a combined mass [1]. For Mars, a calculation published in 2022 estimated approximately 7,119 kg of human-made debris by subtracting the mass of vehicles still operational at the time from the total mass of spacecraft sent to the planet [4]. These figures are estimates, not direct measurements or definitive inventories.

Although this is an important scientific topic, much of the available information is aimed at adult audiences. Children, who may become the next explorers, scientists, and space engineers, rarely find experiences designed to help them understand this issue from their own perspective. Furthermore, not every object left on another world is simply trash: some are scientific equipment or historical artifacts. NASA’s catalog and work on lunar governance emphasize the importance of documenting and protecting these artifacts [1, 6].

Space Junk Explorers turns this topic into an interactive adventure. When they enter the platform, children become astronauts and arrive at a control cabin where they can choose their destination: the Moon or Mars. They then access interactive maps where each location represents an opportunity to make a discovery. Selecting a location activates a mission in which players find an object, discover what it was used for, and learn how it is connected to the space missions that made the exploration of these worlds possible. NASA’s lunar catalog and records of Mars landing debris provide real examples of objects and components that can become part of the exploration experience [1, 5].

The experience includes illustrations, sound effects, clues, and mini-games such as puzzles and exploration challenges. Completing missions unlocks collectible badges and achievements, including Lunar Explorer, Guardian of Mars, and Rover Detective. Every discovery represents progress, and every badge gives players a reason to return and keep exploring. Through this approach, the platform aims to spark children's interest in science, astronomy, and space exploration; encourage curiosity, critical thinking, and independent learning; introduce them to the history of space missions; and raise awareness of objects and materials that remain on other worlds. We hope children will not only learn that these objects exist, but also begin asking questions about them, their history, and the responsibilities that come with space exploration. NASA documentation and analyses of Martian debris show that these objects can have implications for future missions and can also serve as historical milestones [1, 4–6].

The platform was built as a web application using HTML5 (structure), CSS3 (visual design, environments, animations, and interface), and JavaScript (interactions, missions, mini-games, and progression). Netlify was used to publish and host it online. Its content draws on public NASA resources about missions, vehicles, and space artifacts. We also used Claude (Anthropic), an artificial intelligence tool, to help organize ideas, explore alternatives, and support development and writing tasks. The team remained responsible for content selection, project decisions, and final review. The platform runs in a browser without requiring additional installations.

The project's creativity comes from changing where the design process begins. Instead of creating an experience for children based only on what adults think they might find interesting, we decided to ask them directly. We asked Josue, a 7-year-old child, what he would do with the objects left on the Moon and Mars, how he would like to discover them, and what kind of experience he dreamed of having. His answer was not a scientific report; it was an adventure. He told us he wanted a spacecraft where he could be the astronaut and that he wanted to discover the machines. His ideas, drawings, and imagination helped shape the experience, its mechanics, and the way scientific information is presented.

Throughout development, we considered the target audience's age, ease of navigation, language, visual and audio elements, and motivation through rewards. In this way, science stops feeling like a lesson and becomes an adventure children want to continue. Josue was not only the inspiration for the project: he was part of the conversation that made it possible.

Looking ahead, Space Junk Explorers aims to grow with new missions, discoveries, space environments, and educational challenges, introducing more children to the knowledge of our universe. Our purpose goes beyond creating an educational video game: we want to show that science communication can be more approachable, accessible, and participatory when we listen to the people who may shape its future, and that meaningful solutions can emerge when children's imagination and ideas are included from the very beginning.

"Children are not just the audience for the science of the future. They can also be its designers."

[1] NASA History Program Office. (2012). Catalogue of Manmade Material on the Moon. Catalogs human-made lunar artifacts and known locations; it does not provide a consolidated total mass. View NASA catalog.

[2] The Impact of Lunar Dust on Human Exploration, chapter “The Lunar Surface,” p. 137. Gives an approximate estimate of 180,000 kg of human-made material on the lunar surface. View document.

[3] Geggel, L. (March 2, 2018). “How much trash is on the moon?”. Live Science. Reports an estimate of approximately 181,000 kg and notes the uncertainty around the figure. Read article.

[4] Kilic, C. (September 21, 2022). “Mars is littered with 15,694 pounds of human trash from 50 years of robotic exploration”. The Conversation. Estimates 7,119 kg by subtracting the mass of still-operational vehicles from the total mass sent. Read article and calculation.

[5] NASA Science. (August 2, 2022). “Images of EDL Debris”. Documents debris from Perseverance’s entry, descent, and landing system observed on Mars. View NASA Science.

[6] Space Generation Advisory Council. (2023). Effective and Adaptive Governance for a Lunar Ecosystem, submitted to the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space Legal Subcommittee. Describes inactive objects, landers, rovers, and debris on the lunar surface, including their potential heritage value. View UN document.

Scientific accuracy note: lunar figures around 180,000–181,000 kg are published estimates, not an official consolidated NASA total. The 7,119 kg Mars figure is a calculation published in 2022, not a direct weighing or an inventory updated to 2026. NASA’s catalog documents objects and locations but does not sum their mass [1–4].
